learning_goal: Turn the cranial nerve examination from a sequence of twelve remembered manoeuvres into a set of questions each of which has a known anatomical answer. Every test is a circuit with an afferent limb, a centre and an efferent limb, so an abnormal result is read by asking WHICH LIMB failed — and the reflexes are the instrument that separates them, because a reflex with two different nerves in it localises by dissociation: corneal, pupillary, gag and jaw jerk each pair one nerve in with a different nerve out. Then place the failure along the course from `cranial-nerve-courses`: nucleus, nerve, compartment or muscle, using the company a nerve keeps to decide which.

structures.label: Every test is a circuit — ask which limb failed
structures.narration: The examination looks like twelve unrelated manoeuvres and is really one method applied twelve times. Each test drives an input down one nerve and reads an output from another, so an abnormal result is never 'nerve X is broken' until you have asked which limb of the circuit failed. Three ways to ask. First, DISSOCIATION: if a reflex has a different nerve in and out, testing it twice — once from each side — separates them, and that is what makes the corneal, pupillary and gag reflexes the most informative parts of the examination rather than its rituals. Second, COMPANY: nerves that travel together fail together, so the question after 'which nerve' is always 'what else is out', and the answer names the compartment from `cranial-nerve-courses` — the superior orbital fissure, the cavernous sinus, the cerebellopontine angle, the jugular foramen. Third, LEVEL: for the motor nerves, whether the upper face, the palate or the tongue behaves as though the lesion is above or below the nucleus. A cranial nerve examination that produces a compartment rather than a nerve is the one that has been done properly.

structures.label: I and II — smell, acuity, fields, and the pupil as a two-nerve circuit
structures.narration: I is tested one nostril at a time with a smell that is not an irritant — an irritant is trigeminal and would pass with a dead olfactory nerve — and anosmia after head injury is usually the filaments sheared at the cribriform plate. II is tested four ways, and the field is the one that localises: because the nasal fibres cross at the chiasm, a lesion IN FRONT of it takes one eye, a lesion AT it takes both temporal fields (the classic pituitary bitemporal hemianopia), and a lesion BEHIND it takes the same half of both fields. One test, three levels, read off the crossing. Then the pupil, which is the cleanest circuit in the body: light IN along II, out along III to both sides at once, so shining into one eye constricts both. Two consequences. A dead II gives NO response from that eye, direct or consensual, but its pupil still constricts when the OTHER eye is lit — the efferent is intact. A dead III gives no constriction in that eye whichever eye is lit, while the other pupil responds to both. Afferent lesion, both pupils behave the same as each other; efferent lesion, they differ. The swinging flashlight test turns that into a sign: swing the light to the affected eye and the pupil paradoxically dilates, because it is losing more drive than it gains — a relative afferent pupillary defect, the most sensitive test of optic nerve disease there is.

structures.label: III, IV and VI — three nerves, one movement, and where the pupil points
structures.narration: Test them together, because they cannot be separated by the patient's report and can be by the pattern. Trace an H and watch for the eye that fails to reach a corner. VI is simplest: lateral rectus only, so the eye will not abduct and the double vision is worst looking towards the lesion. IV supplies the superior oblique, which turns the eye DOWN when it is already turned IN, so the complaint is double vision going down stairs and the patient tilts the head away from the affected side to compensate. III supplies the other four muscles, the levator and the pupil, so a complete third gives a dilated pupil, a drooping lid and an eye resting DOWN AND OUT — pulled by the two muscles III does not supply, which is why that resting position is diagnostic rather than arbitrary. Then the question that changes management: is the PUPIL involved? Involved means compression from outside — aneurysm, uncal herniation — because the parasympathetic fibres ride on the surface; spared means the microvascular core has infarcted, as in diabetes. And an isolated VI with nothing else is a false localising sign of raised pressure rather than a lesion of the nerve, for the reason `cranial-nerve-courses` gives: it has the longest intracranial course and lies unsupported in the cavernous sinus. All three out together, with a numb forehead, is not three palsies but one cavernous sinus.

structures.label: V and VII — the reflex that separates them, and the sign that levels them
structures.narration: V is tested as three sensory strips and one muscle group: light touch over forehead, cheek and jaw, then clench and open the jaw against resistance — the pterygoids protrude, so a weak V3 lets the jaw DEVIATE TOWARDS the weak side, the same logic as the tongue. The CORNEAL REFLEX is the dissociation test of the face: in along V1, out along VII to both eyes. Touch the affected cornea and if neither eye blinks the afferent V1 is out; if the other eye blinks but this one does not, the efferent VII is out on this side. One reflex, two nerves, told apart by which eye responds. The JAW JERK is the one deep tendon reflex above the neck — in and out along V3 through the mesencephalic nucleus — and it is brisk in an upper motor neuron lesion above the pons, which is how a bilaterally weak face is placed. Then VII, where the single most useful sign in the whole examination lives: ask the patient to raise their eyebrows. The upper face has bilateral cortical input, so a cortical or capsular lesion SPARES the forehead and a lesion of the nerve itself does not. Forehead weak means the nerve; forehead spared means above the nucleus. Add hyperacusis or loss of taste on the front of the tongue and the lesion is inside the facial canal above the branches that carry them, exactly as the course predicts.

structures.label: VIII to XII — hearing, palate, shoulder, tongue
structures.narration: VIII splits into two tests. Hearing: Rinne compares air with bone conduction at one ear and Weber puts the fork on the forehead to compare the two ears. Air better than bone is normal or sensorineural; bone better than air is conductive. Weber lateralises TOWARDS a conductive loss and AWAY from a sensorineural one — the fact worth stating carefully, because a deaf ear that hears the fork loudest is a blocked ear, not a dead nerve. Balance is tested by looking for nystagmus and by the vestibulo-ocular reflex, which involves the same VIII in and III, IV and VI out — another two-nerve circuit. IX and X are tested together because they share the gag: sensation from the pharynx in along IX, elevation of the palate out along X. Say 'ah' and the uvula deviates AWAY from the weak side, because the working side pulls it across — the opposite convention to the tongue, and the pair is worth learning together for exactly that reason. Hoarseness adds the recurrent laryngeal branch of X. XI is tested by shrugging against resistance (trapezius) and turning the head against resistance (sternocleidomastoid), and the crossed action matters: the sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the OPPOSITE side, so a weak right XI is found by failing to turn LEFT. XII: stick the tongue out and it deviates TOWARDS the weak side, since genioglossus protrudes; add wasting and fasciculation and the lesion is the lower motor neuron rather than above it.

views.title: One method, twelve times — in, centre, out
views.narration: Before any manoeuvre, the method. Every test drives an input down one nerve and reads an output from another, so the finding is not a broken nerve until you have said which limb broke. Dissociation separates the limbs of a reflex, company names the compartment, and the level question — forehead, palate, tongue — separates a lesion above the nucleus from one below it. Nothing in this scene is a mesh: it is a drawn set of circuits. The catalog holds no cranial nerve but the two optic ones and no ganglion at all. It does hold the effectors — the muscles of facial expression, the muscles of mastication, sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, and an eyeball — but a test is an ACT rather than a shape: a mesh of orbicularis oculi does not show a blink. Not all of them are absent from disk — the right sternocleidomastoid and the right trapezius are delivered, and so is the whole optic pathway — and they are still not used, because a scene that drew two of its effectors and none of the others would imply the rest had been measured. That is said first so no beat sends a student looking for something absent.

views.title: The pupil — the circuit that tells afferent from efferent
views.narration: Follow the light in along II and out along III to BOTH sides, and every pupillary sign falls out of the wiring. Optic nerve dead: light in that eye moves neither pupil, light in the good eye moves both, and swinging the torch across makes the bad pupil dilate — a relative afferent pupillary defect. Third nerve dead: that pupil moves for no light at all, while the other moves for both. Afferent lesion, the two pupils always match; efferent lesion, they differ. Test the fields in the same breath, because the chiasm turns one manoeuvre into a level: one eye means in front of it, both temporal fields mean at it, the same half of both fields means behind it. And test smell with something that is not an irritant, since an irritant is trigeminal and would be smelt by a patient with no olfactory nerve at all.

views.title: Trace an H — and ask whether the pupil is in
views.narration: Three nerves, one movement, and the pattern of failure names which. No abduction is VI. Trouble looking down and in, with a head tilt away from the side, is IV. A dilated pupil, a ptosis and an eye sitting down and out is a complete III — down and out because those are the pulls of the two muscles III does NOT supply. Then the management question, which is about the pupil and not the eye: involved means compression from outside, since the parasympathetic fibres run on the surface, and that is an aneurysm or a herniation until imaged; spared means the core has infarcted, as in diabetes. Two patterns are not palsies at all: an isolated VI can be raised intracranial pressure stretching the longest intracranial course in the head, and III, IV, VI and a numb forehead together is one cavernous sinus rather than four separate lesions.

views.title: The corneal reflex, and the eyebrow that gives the level
views.narration: Here is dissociation done properly. The corneal reflex goes in along V1 and out along VII to both eyes, so touching the affected cornea answers a different question from touching the other one: neither eye blinks means the sensory V1 is gone; the other eye blinks and this one does not means the motor VII is gone on this side. Test V's three strips and the jaw, which deviates towards the weak side because the pterygoids protrude. Then raise the eyebrows, the single most useful request in the examination: the forehead has bilateral cortical input, so it is SPARED by a lesion above the nucleus and WEAK in a lesion of the nerve. Hyperacusis or lost taste puts that nerve lesion inside the facial canal, above the branches carrying them — the examination reading a level off the course, which is the whole ambition of this scene.

views.title: Fork, uvula, shoulder, tongue — and the two that deviate opposite ways
views.narration: Finish down the list. Rinne at each ear, Weber on the forehead: lateralising towards the bad ear means conductive, away from it means sensorineural. Gag: in along IX, out along X, another two-nerve circuit. Say 'ah' and watch the uvula pull AWAY from the weak side; stick the tongue out and watch it push TOWARDS the weak side. Learn that pair as a pair, because it is the commonest thing to get backwards, and both follow from the same rule — the working muscle wins, and a palate is pulled up while a tongue is pushed out. Shrug and turn the head for XI, remembering the sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side. Wasting and fasciculation of the tongue make the lesion lower motor neuron. Finally, run the company check across the whole examination: IX, X and XI together is a jugular foramen; VII and VIII together with ataxia is a cerebellopontine angle; a cranial nerve on one side with long tracts on the other is the brainstem, as `cranial-nerve-nuclei` derives.

Four facts appear in more than one file and were compared line by line: FOREHEAD SPARING is stated identically here and in `cranial-nerve-courses` (bilateral cortical input to the upper face; forehead weak means the nerve, spared means above the nucleus). THE PUPIL RULE — surface parasympathetic fibres, so compression involves the pupil and microvascular infarction spares it — is stated in both, in the same terms and with the same bounding. THE SIXTH NERVE as a false localising sign is stated in both, with the reason (longest intracranial course, unsupported in the cavernous sinus) given in `cranial-nerve-courses` and referred to here. TONGUE DEVIATION TOWARDS the weak side is stated in `cranial-nerve-nuclei`, `cranial-nerve-courses`, `brainstem__medulla-oblongata` and `spinal-cord__descending-tracts`, and this scene adds the uvula deviating AWAY beside it — the two are given together and each with its mechanism, precisely so that the pair cannot be remembered as a single direction. Nothing here contradicts those files.

TWO STATEMENTS ARE DELIBERATELY BOUNDED. The gag reflex is given as IX in and X out, which is the standard teaching, and the scene does not claim the afferent is purely IX in every subject; and the gag is not described as a test to be performed routinely, because it is unpleasant and often absent normally, so the beat teaches what it would show rather than urging it. The Weber and Rinne interpretation is stated once, in the `lower` card and beat 5 in the same direction (lateralising TOWARDS a conductive loss, AWAY from a sensorineural one), and the two were read against each other this run because this is the single most commonly inverted fact in the examination.
